newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs approve new ferry, plane accident rules.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs approve new ferry, plane accident rules.

text.p: The European Parliament on Wednesday approved two draft EU laws designed to reduce accidents at sea and a third aimed at increasing insurance protection for passengers on European Union air carriers.

Euro-MPs called for the draft directive on compulsory registration of ferry passengers to be extended to cover cars using the Channel Tunnel rail link between Britain and France, which was badly damaged by a fire on a freight train last November.

British Socialist Mark Watts, the author of a report on the passenger safety bill -- COM(96)574 -- has argued that under current Chunnel registration procedures, fire brigades would be unable to tell how many people were trapped in the tunnel if another cross-Channel disaster occurred.

Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock told the EU assembly on Thursday it was not legally possible to extend the scope of the bill to cover the Tunnel but he promised to look into the need for specific legislation on the Folkestone-Calais link.

The new law on ferry passenger lists will bring all 15 countries in the EU bloc into line with a recent International Maritime Organisation (IMO) convention designed to make sailing safer by ensuring the maximum capacity of vessels is not exceeded and making search and rescue operations easier.

The new rules come almost exactly 10 years after Britian's worst ferry disasters, when the Herald of Free Enterprise capsized on a voyage from the English port of Dover and the Belgium port of Zeebrugge.
The ferry sank in about three minutes killing 191 people.

Repeated calls for safety improvements, including an unheeded recommendation by the inquiry into the disaster for the compulsory use of watertight bulkheads, did not prevent another tragedy in 1994 when another roll-on roll-off ferry, the Estonia, sank with the loss of over 900 lives.

"The basic design flaws of ro-ro ferries were not addressed. In fact, competitive pressures, coupled with a lack of comprehensive regulations forced passenger ship owners to cut costs," according to the Watts report, which says some 230 ferries are involved in fatal accidents every year worldwide.

Giving the bill a first reading, parliament urged European transport ministers to introduce a clause obliging the ferry company to make its passenger list available within 30 minutes of sailing, pointing out that the 1987 disaster happened just 22 minutes after the P&O ferry left port.
Euro-MPs also gave a first reading to a draft directive which sets EU-wide minimum training standards for ship crews -- COM(96)470.

The new rules will bring EU regulations into line with a 1995 IMO convention on training, certification and watch- keeping designed to limit human error, which the parliament estimates is the cause of 80 percent of accidents at sea.
Euro-MPs said the rules should also apply to third country vessels using EU ports.
Turning to air travel, the parliament gave a second reading to a draft regulation which increases airlines' liability in the case of accidents -- COM(95)724.
At present, air carrier liability is limited by the 1929 Warsaw Convention to a maximum of $10,000.

The new regulation will waive all financial limits of liability where the airline is at fault, allows passengers to claim compensation of up to 120,000 Ecus ($137,088) even if the carrier did all it could to avoid the accident and provides for advance hardship payments to victims.

Euro-deputies said they realised the EU could not impose the new rules regulation on third country airlines operating in Europe, but said that in the interests of fair competition the EU should seek commitments from them to respect similar levels of liabilty and, at the very least, provide passengers with details of their compensation rules.
EU transport ministers are due to examine all three draft laws at a meeting in Luxembourg on June 17. All three proposals need the support of both parliament and ministers before they can become law.
